1303.title: Two witnesses (Revelation 11)
1303.hook: two prophets killed and raised; the kingdoms become the kingdom of our Lord
1303.howItsDone: Christians speak of bearing witness as telling, plainly and honestly, what they have seen of God, and choirs in churches and concert halls sing Revelation 11:15 in Handel's Hallelujah chorus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the little scroll: honey in John's mouth, bitter once he'd swallowed it. Your line was sweet and bitter.

Two bodies lie in the street of a great city. Nobody is allowed to bury them. People from every nation come to stare, and the mood is a party: neighbors trade gifts, glad these two are finally quiet. They had been prophets in sackcloth, saying what the city didn't want to hear. Then, after three and a half days, something moves. Breath comes back into them. They stand up on their feet, and the watchers are terrified. A voice from heaven calls: come up here. And the two witnesses rise into a cloud while their enemies watch.

Revelation eleven names them plainly: "my two witnesses." A witness says what they've seen, out loud, even when it costs them. First, who are they? They can shut the sky so no rain falls, and turn water into blood. Some readers hear Elijah, who shut the rain, and Moses, who turned the Nile to blood. Others read the two as a picture of the whole witnessing church. The text calls them "the two olive trees, and the two candlesticks standing before the God of the earth," and leaves it there. Second, where they die: in the great city, "where also our Lord was crucified." Their story walks his road: faithful words, a violent death, a watching crowd, and then "the Spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet." Third, the trumpet. Soon after they rise, the seventh angel sounds, and loud voices in heaven say: "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever." Handel set very nearly those words in the Hallelujah chorus of his Messiah. Fourth, the street thought the story was over. The witnesses didn't win by shouting louder. They kept saying what they'd seen. And when they stood, "great fear fell upon them which saw them," and the party went quiet.

A witness isn't loud, just honest about what they've seen. Bring back one good thing you saw with your own eyes, a stranger's kindness, someone who forgave, a prayer that held you up, and hold the faces and the place clearly. If you pray, ask for the chance and the courage to tell it simply; if not, just think of who might need to hear it.
Two witnesses. The prophets of Revelation eleven who speak, are killed, lie in the street, and stand up again when the Spirit of life enters them.
Your line: he shall reign. Heaven's answer to a street that thought the story was over. Same time tomorrow.

1304.title: The woman and the dragon (Revelation 12)
1304.hook: a woman clothed with the sun, a dragon, and a child snatched up to safety
1304.howItsDone: Catholic Christians hear Revelation 12 read on feasts of Mary, and Christian art has pictured her clothed with the sun and crowned with stars; some Protestant preachers read it as the story of God's people kept safe in trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two witnesses stood up in the street, and heaven sang that the kingdoms of this world are his. Your line was he shall reign.

"And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars." She's in labor, crying out. Then a second sign: a great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns, its tail sweeping stars from the sky. It waits in front of her, ready to devour the baby the moment it's born. The child comes, and before the dragon can move, the child is caught up to God and to his throne. The woman runs into the wilderness, to a place God has prepared for her.
screen: `THE CHILD IS CAUGHT UP TO GOD.`

segments.voice: First, who is she? Revelation gives her no name tag, and Christians read her more than one way. Catholic tradition sees in her Mary, the mother of the child who rules, and also the church; Orthodox writers have read her both ways too. Some Protestant readers see God's people: Israel, who brought the Messiah into the world, and the church that follows. Some hold all of these at once. Second, the "war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon." And the dragon "prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven." He's thrown down, and named: that old serpent, the devil. Third, how he's beaten. Not by a bigger dragon. The faithful "overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony." A slain Lamb and people telling the truth. Fourth, the earth helps. The dragon pours a flood from its mouth to sweep the woman away, and "the earth helped the woman, and the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed up the flood." The ground itself takes her side. For all its monsters, the chapter keeps its eye on a mother. Every time she appears, she's in danger: she runs, she hides, she's chased. And she's kept. The dragon doesn't get the child, and it doesn't get her.
screen: `BEATEN BY THE LAMB AND THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind mothers running with their children right now, from war, from a violent home, from hunger, and one woman giving birth tonight with no one safe beside her. If someone you know is carrying a child or a family alone, hold her by name, and if you pray, ask that she be given a place prepared, like the woman in the wilderness. If you're the one who isn't safe at home, you deserve safety: call local emergency help, or in the US, call or text 988.
The woman and the dragon. Revelation twelve's picture of a mother and her child under threat, a dragon thrown down, and a woman kept safe in the wilderness.

1305.title: The beasts (Revelation 13)
1305.hook: empire as a beast demanding worship; many read 666 as a code for Nero
1305.howItsDone: Christians read Revelation 13 in different ways: some as a word about Rome in John's own day, some as a pattern that repeats whenever power asks to be worshiped, and some as a picture of events still to come.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman clothed with the sun, a dragon thrown down, and the earth swallowing a flood. Your line was the dragon loses.

Six hundred threescore and six. That number has set off a great deal of guessing, and it comes from one verse at the end of Revelation thirteen. But before the number, there's a crowd. A beast has risen out of the sea, and the whole world follows it in wonder. People bow down, chanting the kind of question you shout at a rally: "Who is like unto the beast? who is able to make war with him?" Today's word is that beast, and the one that comes after it.

First, the chant is borrowed. After the sea crossing in Exodus, Moses and Israel sang: "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?" The crowd takes a song meant for God and sings it to a beast. That's the beast's whole project: to be worshiped. It's given power, the text says, over every kindred and tongue and nation. Second, another beast comes up out of the earth: "he had two horns like a lamb, and he spake as a dragon." It looks gentle and sounds like something else. Its job is to make everyone worship the first beast, and to see that no one can buy or sell without its mark. Third, the number: "Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man." Some readers hear a code for Nero, the Roman emperor. Others read a symbol: a number that keeps falling short. Others again wait for a figure still to come. The text itself only says it is the number of a man. Fourth, what John says to do. Not panic, not decode: "Here is the patience and the faith of the saints." Some readers carry the chapter into ordinary life: the beast need not look like a monster. It can be any power that asks for more than loyalty, that wants worship. And it can look like a lamb.
screen: `A SONG FOR GOD, SUNG TO A BEAST.`
`HORNS LIKE A LAMB, VOICE OF A DRAGON.`

segments.voice: Think back over the week to where something asked more of you than it should: a job that wants your whole evening, a screen that wants you every few minutes, a leader, a party or a crowd that asks you never to question it. Don't judge yourself; just see it plainly, the way John saw a lamb's horns and heard a dragon's voice. If you pray, name it to God and give your loyalty back where you believe it belongs; if not, name it to yourself.
The beasts. In Revelation thirteen, one from the sea that wants worship, and one from the earth that looks like a lamb and speaks like a dragon.
Your line: don't bow to the beast. Patience and faith, not panic. Rest well.

1306.title: The harvest (Revelation 14)
1306.hook: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord; they rest from their labors
1306.tomorrow: The song of Moses and the Lamb
1306.howItsDone: Christians pray for or remember their dead at funerals and on days set aside for them, and Revelation 14:13 is read in some burial services; churches differ on praying for the dead, with Catholic and Orthodox Christians praying for them directly and some Protestants giving thanks for them instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beasts, and one with a lamb's horns and a dragon's voice. Your line was don't bow to the beast.

A funeral on a gray afternoon. People in dark coats stand around an open grave. The minister opens a worn book and reads lines that sound older than everyone there: a voice from heaven, telling John to write. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. They rest from their labors. And their works follow them. Those words sit in the middle of Revelation fourteen, a chapter of flying angels, a sickle, and a field ready to be cut. Today's word is that field.

First, a mountain. The Lamb stands on Mount Sion with his people, and they sing a new song no one else can learn. After yesterday's beasts, the Lamb is still standing. Second, the voice: "Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them." Notice the order. Rest first. Then their works follow, like a family walking behind a coffin. Nothing good they did is lost. The old Anglican Book of Common Prayer sets this verse in its burial service, read at the grave. Third, the harvest. John sees one "like unto the Son of man" on a white cloud with a sharp sickle, and an angel calls: "Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe." Jesus told stories like this: wheat and weeds growing together until the harvest. Here it comes. A second harvest follows, grapes thrown into a winepress, a hard picture of judgment. Some readers take it literally; others hear picture language. Fourth, for anyone who has buried someone who died in faith, the chapter says two things at once: those who die in the Lord are at rest, and their works are not left behind. The harvest is when what was growing is finally gathered in.

Let one person who has died come to mind, a grandparent, a friend, someone you never got to say goodbye to, and see their face. Think of one good thing of theirs that still follows them: a recipe you still cook, a habit of kindness, a phrase you catch yourself saying. If you pray, commend them to God by name and ask that they rest; if not, thank them silently. And if grief is heavy today, you don't have to carry it alone: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
The harvest. In Revelation fourteen, the field of the earth gathered in at the end, and the dead who die in the Lord at rest, with their works following them.
Your line: they rest from their labors. And their works follow them. Go gently today.

1307.title: The song of Moses and the Lamb (Revelation 15–16)
1307.word: The song of Moses and the Lamb
1307.hook: by a sea of glass, they sing: great and marvelous are your works
1307.howItsDone: Christians sing praise in worship, and some churches sing the words of Revelation 15:3–4 as a canticle; the song at the sea from Exodus 15 also has a place in Jewish morning prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harvest, and a voice saying the dead in the Lord rest, their works following them. Your line was they rest from their labors.

On the far shore of the Red Sea, the water has just closed. Under it lies the army that chased them; ahead, a desert. And Moses and the people of Israel sing: "I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea." Miriam picks up a tambourine and the women dance. Now jump to near the end of the Bible. John sees another sea, made of glass and shot through with fire. People stand on it, harps in their hands, through their own long chase. And they sing too.
screen: `A SEA OF GLASS, MINGLED WITH FIRE.`

segments.voice: Revelation fifteen calls it "the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb." One song, two names. First, the old song comes back. Two days ago the beast's crowd borrowed a line from it; here it's sung to God again. Israel sang after coming through the sea out of slavery; these singers sing after the Lamb has brought them through. John hears the Exodus and the story of Jesus as one song. Second, the words: "Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints." Not about the singers, or what they survived, or how brave they were. Every line is about God. Third, the song looks outward: "for all nations shall come and worship before thee." They've just escaped, and they're already singing about everybody else coming in. Fourth, what comes next is hard. In chapter sixteen seven angels pour out bowls, and the plagues sound like Egypt again: sores, water turned to blood, darkness, and unclean spirits like frogs. Some readers hear the Exodus told once more, on a bigger stage. Twice the text says the people under the plagues still would not repent. So the song isn't sung because life is easy. In Acts, Paul and Silas sing praises in a prison at midnight. Praise here isn't a reward for things going well. It's what the rescued do on the shore, between the chase and the desert.
screen: `SUNG BETWEEN THE CHASE AND THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Sing a hymn you know, a psalm you've heard sung, or any song that says thank you for the world: out loud if you can, humming or inside you if not. Don't worry about your voice; let the song be about what's great and good, not about you. If you pray, let it be your prayer; if not, let it simply be a song.
The song of Moses and the Lamb. In Revelation fifteen, the song sung beside a sea of glass, echoing Israel's song at the Red Sea: great and marvelous are your works.

1308.title: Babylon falls (Revelation 17–18)
1308.hook: the merchants weep over a city that trafficked in bodies and souls
1308.howItsDone: Some Christians read Revelation 18 as a call to look at how goods are made and traded, and churches and Christian groups run fair-trade stalls and campaigns against human trafficking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a song by a sea of glass, the song of Moses and the Lamb. Your line was great and marvelous.

A shipping manifest sits in the middle of Revelation eighteen, and it reads like one. Gold, silver, precious stones, pearls. Fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet. Ivory, bronze, iron, marble. Cinnamon, incense, ointments, frankincense. Wine, oil, fine flour, wheat. Cattle, sheep, horses, chariots. And at the very end, two more items of cargo. The merchants who traded it all stand at a distance, watching a great city burn, and weep. The reason the text gives for their tears: nobody is buying their goods anymore. Today's word is that city's end.

First, the city. In chapter seventeen Babylon is a woman in purple and scarlet, riding a beast, drunk on the blood of the saints. Babylon once carried the people of Jerusalem into exile, and in Revelation the name becomes a code. Some readers hear Rome, the city of seven hills; others hear any city or empire that grows rich by using people up. Second, the cry: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen." Then the mourners: "Alas, alas that great city Babylon, that mighty city! for in one hour is thy judgment come." Kings, merchants, sailors: everyone who profited mourns. Third, the end of the list. The King James closes the cargo with "and slaves, and souls of men." The Greek word behind slaves there is the word for bodies. Bodies and human souls, listed after the horses and chariots as if they were the same kind of thing. Some readers hear that as the heart of the charge: Babylon put people on the inventory. Fourth, the call. Before the fire, a voice from heaven: "Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins." Christians have heard it as leaving a place, or as refusing its rules while still inside it. Some readers say Babylon is never far: in the clothes, the phones, the food, wherever a price is low because someone, somewhere, was treated like cargo.

Look at what's around you, your shirt, your coffee, the phone in your hand, pick one thing, and wonder without guilt whose hands touched it before yours. Then choose one thing you'll buy this week, and decide to look for a version made by people who were paid and treated fairly. If you pray, pray for the people whose hands made your things; if not, just hold them in mind.
Babylon falls. In Revelation seventeen and eighteen, the great trading city collapses in one hour, and its cargo list ends with bodies and human souls.
Your line: bodies and souls. The last two items on Babylon's list. I'll be here tomorrow.

1309.title: The marriage supper (Revelation 19)
1309.hook: blessed are those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb
1309.howItsDone: In some churches, the words of Revelation 19:9 are said at communion, just before people come to the table, and Christian weddings and feast-day meals are described by some as a foretaste of the wedding feast of the Lamb.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Babylon fell, and its cargo list ended with people. Your line was bodies and souls.

Smoke is still rising from Babylon. Then a sound comes over it, and John describes it three ways: like a great crowd, like rushing water, like thunder. What they're shouting isn't a war cry. It's a word you may have sung yourself: "Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth." Then they say why they're so happy. Not a battle. A wedding. "The marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready." After all the seals and trumpets and bowls and beasts, Revelation's next great scene of joy is a party.

First, two women. Yesterday's Babylon wore purple and scarlet, decked with gold. Today's bride wears something plainer: "to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints." Notice the word granted. The verse before says she made herself ready; this one says the linen was given to her. Churches weigh those two lines differently. Christian tradition reads the bride as the people of God, the church, married to the Lamb. Second, the invitation: "Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb." Jesus told stories about this feast. In Matthew, "The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son," and the invitations go out to the streets. In John's Gospel, the beginning of his signs was at a wedding in Cana, when the wine ran out. His signs begin at a wedding, and Revelation arrives at one. Third, John gets it wrong. Overwhelmed, he falls at the angel's feet to worship. The angel stops him: "See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant." Worship God. Fourth, the shape of hope here. Not only escape, or rest, or a verdict. A table: a meal with people you love, with music and too much food. Some Christians at communion speak of tasting that feast ahead of time; churches understand the meal differently, and some set the table with this hope in view.
screen: `A BRIDE IN LINEN, GIVEN TO HER.`
`EVEN THE ANGEL IS A FELLOW SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Picture your next meal with someone, tonight or this week, and what would make it feel like a feast without costing much: a candle, a cloth, flowers from outside, phones put away, someone who rarely gets invited. See the table set, the people around it, the noise. If you pray, give thanks for it ahead of time; if not, just enjoy the picture.
The marriage supper. In Revelation nineteen, the wedding feast of the Lamb and his bride, and the blessing on everyone called to it.
Your line: the wedding feast. From two witnesses in the street, past a dragon, beasts, a harvest, a song and a fallen city, this week ended at a wedding. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Is Revelation all doom? What's the big happy moment near the end?
options: A wedding: heaven shouts alleluia, and the Lamb's marriage supper begins, with a blessing on the guests.
A battle: the saints cheer as their enemies burn, and that's the last word of the whole book.
A coronation: the angel John bows to is crowned as the king of the whole new world.
chat.meaning: After Babylon falls, the crowd shouts alleluia because the marriage of the Lamb has come: "Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper."

Alleluia.meaning: a Hebrew shout of praise: praise the Lord

Cana.meaning: the village where Jesus's first sign happened, at a wedding

fellowservant.meaning: old English for one who serves alongside you

communion.meaning: the shared bread and cup of Christian worship
